It's not just President Trump barnstorming key states in the closing days of the midterms. The Democrats have several high-profile surrogates hitting the campaign trail as well. One example: former President Barack Obama will be in Ohio and Michigan this weekend and Georgia next week. He says special committees have been set up at each of the companies to discuss it. And analysts say it actually could make some business sense. You know, for example, Tesla makes solar panels and Batteries that are used in SpaceX satellites. SpaceX runs the Starlink satellite internet system that Tesla's self-driving cars use. They're working on a chip factory together. Ryan Mulberry is chief market strategist for Zach's Investment Management, which holds shares in both companies. Combining the balance sheets and making one company allows Tesla to use that intellectual property, that design and engineering, without without having to lease it or write a check, if you will, from the right hand to the left hand in order to be able to use that type of technology. Both companies are developing AI too and spending a lot of money on it. And analysts say there could be advantages to putting all that under one roof. What would be in it for Musk? Well, these are both essential parts of Musk's vision for a tech-enabled future that involves things like robots and space-based data centers. So a merger could give him more control over that. Musk holds nearly half of SpaceX shares and over 80% of shareholder voting power. With Tesla, he has a lot less voting power. And so if these companies merge into one, analysts think he could come out of it with a controlling share. The other thing for Moscow, of course, is money. In November, Tesla shareholders approved a trillion-dollar pay package for him contingent upon meeting some growth targets in the next decade. Analysts think a merger could make it easier for him to hit those targets and get the payout. What could it take to make this merger happen? Shareholders would have to approve any deal. That might be a challenge on the Tesla side, where half of all shareholders would have to be in favor of it. Analysts think they could demand a higher share price. Some institutional investors might not love the idea of forfeiting more control to Musk. Also, Tesla has bigger revenues than SpaceX, so those would be diluted in a combined company. And shareholders who invested in Tesla because they like EVs would have to get really comfortable owning shares in a company with a lot more businesses like Rockets, Starlink, the Grok chatbot, the social media site X. Seth Goldstein, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar, says there are also regulatory hurdles. Tesla makes cars in China. SpaceX does work with the Pentagon. The U.S. government may not like having a U.S. defense contractor that's relying on the Chinese government for its key manufacturing operations. And likewise, Beijing may also not be so keen on an American defense contractor operating in China or running self-driving cars there.
